title: What is known about 1RB1RF_1LC0LB_1RE1LD_1RE0LB_1RA0RE_---0RC
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RF_1LC0LB_1RE1LD_1RE0LB_1RA0RE_---0RC.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open, but reduced to one lemma. The machine is a binary counter that gains 39 or 42 every 8 sweeps. Lean proves that every sweep keeps the counter in its steady form except at a B-overflow (once every second doubling), so a halt would have to happen in a B-overflow transient; the run through the first one is evaluated too. Proving that every B-overflow transient ends well (its long exit sweep, about 140·2w steps with two nested counters) would prove non-halting.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: Where a halt can come from
claims.text: If the machine halts on its third step from a configuration, that configuration is one of: E with 0 under the head, 1 right, 0 two right. So a run can reach a halt only through one of these patterns, and a proof that the machine never halts only has to rule them out. The proof splits on the state and the five cells around the head.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 63,134 cells have been visited and 32,679 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: fixed/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.514).

claims.title: Tape structure
claims.text: At 108 steps the tape ends in (0111)^3998 011 A>1 (1001)^907 1, at 109 in (1011)^1088 10 B>1 (0110)^14656 011: two long periodic blocks meet at the head and trade length, with an irregular region of short words to their left that changes slowly.

claims.title: The two sweeps across the long block
claims.text: L (1011)^n 1 0 C> 0^inf reaches L C> 1 (1001)^n 10011 0^inf in 4n+8 steps, and L 1 F> (1001)^n 10011 0^inf reaches L 1 (0111)^n 01110 C> 0^inf in 4n+5 steps, for all n and every tape L.

claims.title: Every sweep that does not overflow the counter
claims.text: The middle part of each visit (between the two block crossings) is proved for all 7 shallow cases (inner counter i < 7, i → i+1) and all 162 deep cases (i = 7: V → V + 39 or 42, t flips), for every value of the five low digits, digit 5 when it matters, and a carry crossing any number of 1-digits, for every tape left of the digit that stops the carry. With back/forth these cover every visit that does not overflow V.

claims.title: The counter model holds for 2·10<sup>10</sup> steps
claims.text: c/visits.c parses every visit (head in state C on the blank cell right of the tape) as [1] U(b_top)..U(b_1) b_0 0 1 M(t) I(i) (1011)^m 1 0 and checks each pair of consecutive visits against the rule; 70,664 visits, 0 exceptions; 5 A-overflows and 4 B-overflow transients (8-32 visits each) all behave as described in the README.

claims.title: The A-overflows
claims.text: A deep visit in phase A whose carry runs through all digits to the blank tape (0^inf (U(1))^(k+1) [U(b5)] low M(t) I(7)) ends as phase B with the same width and a lone 1 in front (0^inf 1 (U(0))^(k+1) [U(b5)] low' M(1-t) I(0)), for all 81 cases and every k.

claims.title: Every steady visit that is not a B-overflow leads to a steady visit
claims.text: The visit configurations are written with the digits of V as a list of bits; Steady says the tape has the steady layout (phase A or B, at least 7 digits, block at least as long as the counter is wide). For every such configuration that is not a B-overflow, the run reaches another steady configuration: shallow visits, deep visits with a carry through any number of 1-digits, and A-overflows, for every counter value, width and block length.

claims.title: A halt can only come in a B-overflow transient, and not in the first one
claims.text: The run from blank tape reaches a steady visit (visit 280, step 1,882,602, evaluated), so with steady_step a halt needs the run to reach a steady B-overflow visit first; the run through the first B-overflow transient to visit 2688 (step 31,879,658) is evaluated too, so that B-overflow must come at step 31,879,658 or later.

claims.title: Non-halting follows from one lemma about the B-overflows
claims.text: If every steady B-overflow visit is followed by a steady visit, the machine never halts from blank tape.

claims.title: Every B-overflow transient up to its exit sweep
claims.text: The symbolic simulator runs all 81 possible B-overflows (switch t, five low digits, digit 5 when they carry) for any number of digits and any block length: 0 to 48 ordinary-looking transient sweeps, in which a small counter written into M is incremented instead of V, and then the exit sweep, where it stops because an inner counter carries into the zero digits.

claims.title: The exit sweep
claims.text: In the four B-overflows of the run (w = 13 to 16) the exit sweep takes about 140.5·2<sup>w</sup> extra steps. It is a loop of rounds of about 140 steps: each round adds 3 to a binary counter in the digit cells (at w = 13: from 14 to 2<sup>13</sup> in 2,726 rounds, then, one bit wider, from 0 to 2<sup>14</sup> − 1 in 5,461 more), while a second counter (base-3 digits in M, continued on the first copies of the block) counts the rounds. After a final loop and a clean-up it ends at a steady phase-A visit with one more digit and V = 2<sup>w</sup> + 203, 323, 203, 242. The round counter, the final loop and the clean-up are decoded only roughly.

claims.title: It never halts
claims.text: A halt can only happen in a B-overflow exit sweep. That sweep is a fixed program run on counters whose lengths grow with the width, the four seen behave alike, the symbolic runs reach it in all 81 cases, and 2·10<sup>10</sup> steps follow the model with no exception, so a halt is very unlikely.

claims.title: Regular-language deciders tried (F11)
claims.text: None of these closes: each reaches a halting configuration in its abstraction, which says nothing about whether the machine halts. n-gram CPS (tools/c/ngramcps.c), equal widths on both sides: a halting local configuration is reached with plain up to width 18, history 1 up to width 14, history 2 up to width 13, history 3 up to width 11, LRU history up to width 13 (larger widths ran out of the 150 s or 60 million configuration budget). n-gram CPS with every cell tagged by its position mod p: fails for p = 2 up to width 16, p = 3 up to width 20, p = 4 up to width 20, p = 6 up to width 20. Run-length windows (the K nearest runs of equal macro cells on each side, run lengths kept exactly below T and mod M above): fails for all 72 parameter sets (cells of 1 to 4 bits, K = 2, 4, 6, T = 2, 4, M = 1, 2, 4). Two-automaton closed tape language by SAT (a deterministic automaton reading each side inward, n states each, CaDiCaL): no solution for n = 2..8; n = 9 not finished in 150 s.
claims.where: sweeps of 13 November 2026 (family F11); the tagged and run-length deciders are not in the repository yet

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not proved. Missing: the hypothesis of nonhalting_of_transients, that every B-overflow transient ends at a steady visit; the hard part is the exit sweep (an induction over the rounds of its inner loop, for 78 different start configurations). See Next steps in the README.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Started on a blank tape, this Turing machine has run for 10<sup>9</sup> steps without stopping. This page runs the real machine in your browser, shows the shape of its run, and lists what is known, each result marked by what it rests on.

facts.text: Proved in Lean: a halt can only happen inside a B-overflow transient (once per two doublings of the counter), and not in the first one.
No halt in the C simulator; 63,134 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
The growth shape of the two sides of the tape (see below).

sections.heading: A counter that counts by 81 every 16 sweeps
html: The head sweeps from one end of the tape to the other and back. Look at the tape each time the head arrives at the right end (a visit): it always has the same layout.

<svg viewBox='0 0 560 96' role='img' aria-label='the tape at a visit: lone 1, the digits of V, M(t), I(i), the long block, the head' style='width:100%;max-width:560px;height:auto;font:12px var(--mono)'><rect x='10' y='20' width='14' height='26' fill='var(--muted)'/><rect x='24' y='20' width='150' height='26' fill='var(--head)'/><text x='99' y='37' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--bg)'>digits of V</text><rect x='174' y='20' width='70' height='26' fill='var(--accent)'/><text x='209' y='37' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--bg)'>M(t)</text><rect x='244' y='20' width='46' height='26' fill='var(--fg2)'/><text x='267' y='37' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--bg)'>I(i)</text><rect x='290' y='20' width='240' height='26' fill='var(--ink)'/><text x='410' y='37' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--bg)'>(1011)^m, +1 copy per sweep</text><text x='540' y='37' fill='var(--fg2)'>C</text><text x='99' y='66' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--fg2)'>+39 or +42</text><text x='99' y='82' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>every 8 sweeps</text><text x='209' y='66' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--fg2)'>t flips</text><text x='267' y='66' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--fg2)'>i+1 mod 8</text><text x='10' y='14' fill='var(--muted)'>phase B only</text></svg>

• At the left, a number V written in binary, one digit per 6 cells (b01101, where b is the digit).
  • Then a fixed 45-cell word M(t) with one switch cell t, and a 3-digit counter i written the same way.
  • Then the long block (1011)^m, one copy longer at each visit.

At each visit i goes up by one. When it wraps from 7 to 0, the head walks all the way into V and adds 39 to it (if t = 0) or 42 (if t = 1), and t flips. So V grows by 81 every 16 visits, carries ripple left exactly as when you add on paper.

Overflows

When V runs out of digits something special happens. The first time (phase A to phase B), the digits are rewritten one cell to the right with a lone 1 in front. The second time (a B-overflow, phase B to phase A), after a transient of up to 48 visits and one very long sweep, V has one more digit. Each such cycle takes twice as long as the previous one, so the left end of the tape grows only like the logarithm of the time.

sections.heading: Everything except one kind of overflow
html: Each sweep is cut into three pieces: crossing the block leftwards, the turn-around in M, I and the low digits of V, and crossing the block back. The two crossings are proved in Lean for blocks of any length. The turn-around is proved in 250 separate theorems: 7 for the ordinary visits (i < 7), 162 for the adding visits (one for each value of the five lowest digits of V, the switch t, and whether a carry goes further, which also covers carries running through any number of 1-digits), and 81 for the first kind of overflow, where the carry runs off the left end of the counter.

Then the pieces are glued together. A predicate Steady describes the tape at a visit: the digits of V as a list of bits, M, I and the block. One theorem, steady_step, says: from any steady visit the machine gets to another steady visit, unless the visit starts the second kind of overflow (a B-overflow). It is proved by looking at the low digits and at the first 0-digit above them, and picking the right one of the 250 theorems. The start from blank tape to the first steady visit (1,882,602 steps) is computed.

Proved: if the machine ever halts, it does so inside a B-overflow, and not inside the first one (at step 30 million, also computed in Lean). Proved: if every B-overflow ends in a steady visit again, the machine never halts.
So the whole question comes down to the B-overflows. They are rare (the counter must double twice between two of them) but complicated, see the next section.

sections.heading: The B-overflow: a sweep that takes millions of steps
html: When V overflows in phase B, all its digits become 0. For the next 0 to 48 visits nothing special seems to happen, except that the adding visits now add to a small counter hidden inside M instead of V. When that counter fills up, comes the exit sweep: the head walks to V and does not come back for about 140·2w steps (1.16 million when V has 13 digits, 9.2 million at 16).

<svg viewBox='0 0 560 110' role='img' aria-label='the exit sweep: a binary counter in the digit cells and a second counter in M and on the block, both counting rounds' style='width:100%;max-width:560px;height:auto;font:12px var(--mono)'><rect x='10' y='24' width='170' height='26' fill='var(--head)'/><text x='95' y='41' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--bg)'>digits: +1 per round</text><rect x='180' y='24' width='120' height='26' fill='var(--accent)'/><text x='240' y='41' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--bg)'>base-3 digits in M</text><rect x='300' y='24' width='80' height='26' fill='var(--fg2)'/><text x='340' y='41' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--bg)'>base-4</text><rect x='380' y='24' width='170' height='26' fill='var(--ink)'/><text x='465' y='41' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--bg)'>rest of the block</text><path d='M95 60 C 95 95, 240 95, 240 60' fill='none' stroke='var(--fg2)'/><text x='170' y='104' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--fg2)'>one round, about 140 steps</text><text x='340' y='16' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>written over block copies</text></svg>

Inside this sweep the machine runs a little program of its own: every round of about 140 steps it adds 3 to a binary counter in the digit cells and 1 to a second counter to the right, written in base 3 in the cells of M and continued over the first copies of the long block. The digit counter runs up to its limit, gains one digit, runs up to the new limit (when V has 13 digits: 2,726 rounds and then 5,461 more), and then the tape is tidied up into the steady layout with V one digit wider.

A computer program that simulates the machine with letters for unknown lengths runs every one of the 81 possible B-overflows up to the exit sweep. What is missing is a proof that the exit sweep always ends well: an induction over the rounds of its inner loop, with two counters whose carries both have to be followed.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.514).
After 109 steps the tape spans 63,134 cells (82 left of the start, 46,087 right), with a density of 1s of 0.518.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machines below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in any of the others, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

  • 1RB0LD_1RC0RB_1RD1RF_1LE0LD_1RB1LA_---0RE: rename A→C, B→D, C→E, D→A, E→B, F→F; it is this table started in state D
  • 1RB0RA_1RC1RF_1LD0LC_1RA1LE_1RA0LC_---0RD: rename A→B, B→C, C→D, D→E, E→A, F→F; it is this table started in state E

summary: A binary counter at the left end gaining 39 or 42 every 8 sweeps, next to a block that grows each sweep; proved in Lean that it can halt only inside a B-overflow transient (once per two doublings of the counter), and not in the first; that transient's long exit sweep is not proved; open, almost certainly non-halting.
family: binary counter (+39/+42 per 8 sweeps) with growing block
